sections.readerQuestion: What is this page about, whose contribution is it and why should I read it?
sections.usefulAnswer: Andy Galpin says cyclists over 40 still have the capacity to improve strength and power. In his Roadman interview he distinguishes learning a new exercise from improving a well-trained cycling task, and explains why riding volume, sleep and energy availability matter. The practical starting point is to define the intended outcome and record gym progress and cycling performance separately.

sections.readerQuestion: What is this page about, whose contribution is it and why should I read it?
sections.usefulAnswer: A beginner cyclist can start with two non-consecutive full-body strength sessions per week, using one or two work sets per movement and several good repetitions in reserve. Weeks 1–2 learn and tolerate; weeks 3–6 build a repeatable two-session routine; weeks 7–12 progress selected movements while priority rides remain productive. Cover knee-dominant, hip-dominant, upper-body and trunk patterns, with single-leg or calf work when useful. This is a conservative Roadman framework, not the single 12-week protocol proved by a cyclist study.

sections.readerQuestion: What is this page about, whose contribution is it and why should I read it?
sections.usefulAnswer: Heavy strength training can improve cycling performance, cycling efficiency and anaerobic power. In the latest cyclist-only meta-analysis, programmes used loads of at least 80% of one-repetition maximum for 5–25 weeks and 1–3 sessions per week. The certainty of evidence was low, however, and the review did not establish one best frequency, exercise list or year-round protocol. For many riders, two non-consecutive sessions per week is a practical starting point—not a proven universal minimum—followed by lower volume when riding or racing load rises.

sections.readerQuestion: What is this page about, whose contribution is it and why should I read it?
sections.usefulAnswer: Art O’Connor explains how he coaches strength alongside cycling. He starts by looking at movement quality, uses a range of lower-body, upper-body and trunk exercises, and adjusts the work to the rider. His suggestion to combine demanding gym work with hard riding days is intended to preserve easier days. His session frequencies and exercise examples describe coaching practice; they do not establish one optimal schedule for every cyclist.

claimsAndSources: Galpin and O’Connor summaries were checked against the original imported transcript strings, which remain unchanged. Fabricated-looking quotations and unsupported claims were removed. Galpin current affiliation is supported by Parker University. Chris Peden has original listing metadata and a playable Spotify reference only. PMID 40632222 is described as low-certainty cyclist research. Existing archived episode durations remain historical metadata and are not used to manufacture clip timestamps.
examplesAndReasoning: The guides ask the reader to name a priority ride, compare gym slots, record work and effort, and assess cycling separately. They do not invent client outcomes or exact schedules that the interviews did not establish. The source-to-waitlist flow uses fixed editorial identifiers and retains consent-aware CTA click handling; a click is not a confirmed signup or an install.
voiceAndCuts: Removed unsupported fast-twitch/protein prescriptions, fabricated quotations, universal optimal frequency, zero-recovery-cost claims, invented founder recollections and repeated sales modules on selected pages. Used plain explanations and directly linked original sources. Final rendered reading also cut two redundant rhetorical sentences from the companion articles.
desktopReview: In progress: authenticated branch preview accessible. The first actual desktop review at 1363 × 936 caught a broken external product image and an injected newsletter splitting the founder quotation. Both are corrected in source and await rendered verification. No final desktop pass yet.
mobileReview: In progress: actual preview iframe measured 390 × 844. Initial /app hero has no horizontal overflow. Final revised image and all selected reading/CTA layouts still require verification.
productAndOfferAccuracy: Good Legs is in development for iPhone with an open beta waitlist, no promised invitation, public launch date or standalone price. Not Done Yet access is at launch. Guest appearances are editorial sources rather than product endorsements. Current product capabilities were checked against Roadman product definitions and the original product website source.
